home.heroDescription: Access the university's official training modules for Fundamentals of Computer Science.

automata.title: Finite Automata
automata.description: Study deterministic and non-deterministic finite automata. Build DFAs and NFAs, convert regular grammars, and step through input words.
automata.overviewText: Finite Automata are the simplest computational models used to recognize patterns. They consist of states, transitions, and accept/reject decisions. DFAs and NFAs form the foundation for lexical analysis, pattern matching, and regular expression engines.
automata.concept1Desc: Build either type — the editor flags non-determinism in your transition table.
automata.concept2Desc: Paste a right-linear regular grammar and convert it to an NFA in one click.
automata.dfaPoint2: Exactly one active state at any time
automata.nfaPoint2: Set of active states explored in parallel
automata.feature1: Build DFAs and NFAs visually using a transition table
automata.feature2: Convert a right-linear regular grammar into an automaton
automata.feature3: Step through an input word and watch the state diagram update
automata.feature4: Batch-test multiple words and inspect accept/reject results
automata.exercise1Desc: Create a DFA that accepts strings ending in '01'
automata.exercise2Desc: Design an NFA for a given regular expression

number.title: Number Systems
number.description: Master conversions between Binary, Octal, Decimal, and Hexadecimal. Understand IEEE 754 floating-point representation.
number.overviewText: Number systems are fundamental to how computers store and process data. Understanding binary, octal, and hexadecimal representations is essential for low-level programming, networking, and digital design.
number.ex_u03_binAddDesc: Convert two decimal numbers to binary and add them.
number.ex_u04_binToHexOctDesc: Convert 8-bit binary numbers to hex and octal.
number.ex_u05_floatToBinDesc: Convert simple floating point numbers to binary.
number.ex_u05_ieeeEncodeDesc: Convert float values to the 32-bit IEEE 754 standard.
number.ex_u05_ieeeDecodeDesc: Calculate the decimal value of an IEEE 754 32-bit string.
number.examplesFallback: Interactive examples for Number Systems will be available here.
number.example_u03_1_desc: Convert the decimal number 26 to binary.
number.example_u03_2_desc: Add the numbers 50 and 13 as binary numbers.
number.example_u04_1_desc: Represent the binary number 01111010 as a hexadecimal number.
number.example_u04_2_desc: Represent the binary number 0011 1100 as an octal number.
number.example_u04_3_desc: Represent the octal number 760 as a hexadecimal number.
number.example_u04_4_desc: Represent the hexadecimal number 7F as a binary number.
number.example_u05_1_desc: Convert the decimal number 10.5 to a binary floating point number.
number.example_u05_2_desc: Represent 3.375 as a normalized binary floating point number.

moore.title: Moore & Mealy Machines
moore.description: Explore sequential circuit design with Moore and Mealy state machines. Learn the differences and when to apply each model.
moore.overviewText: Moore and Mealy machines are finite state machines with output. In Moore machines, output depends only on the current state. In Mealy machines, output depends on both the current state and the current input. Both are fundamental to digital circuit design.
moore.exercise1Desc: Create a sequence detector as Moore machine
moore.exercise2Desc: Create a sequence detector as Mealy machine
moore.exercise3Desc: Convert a Moore machine to equivalent Mealy
moore.exercise4Desc: Convert a Mealy machine to equivalent Moore

dnf.title: Disjunctive Normal Form
dnf.description: Learn how boolean expressions are evaluated with truth tables and how the Disjunctive Normal Form is derived from the rows with result 1.
dnf.overviewText: Disjunctive Normal Form (DNF) writes a boolean expression as OR-linked AND terms. In the lecture style, each truth-table row with result 1 contributes exactly one term.
dnf.examplesIntro: Examples for both modes: from expression to truth table, and from truth table to DNF.

lectureExpression.title: Expression with an AND group
lectureExpression.explanation: The expression is true when a=1 or b and c are both 1.

parentheses.title: Parentheses change the result
parentheses.explanation: Here c=1, and a=1 or b=1 must also hold.

negation.title: Negation restricts the true rows
negation.explanation: Because ¬a is set, only rows with a=0 can be true. Additionally, b or c must equal 1.

xor.title: Half-adder sum as XOR
xor.explanation: The sum is 1 when exactly one input is 1.

carry.title: Half-adder carry
carry.explanation: The carry bit is only 1 when both inputs are 1 — a single AND term.

dnfIntro.title: DNF introduction from the lecture
dnfIntro.explanation: Only rows 000 and 111 evaluate to 1, producing two AND terms.

exerciseTwo.title: Exercise 2: polynomial from truth table
exerciseTwo.explanation: Three 1-rows (010, 100, 101) lead to the DNF of lecture exercise 2.

dnf.exampleExpressionText: The expression is true as soon as a is true or b and c are true together.
dnf.exampleRuleText: If the value is 1, keep the variable as-is; if the value is 0, negate it. This makes each AND term describe exactly one matching table row.

topic.title: Turing Machines
topic.description: Learn about the fundamentals of computation through Turing Machines and their transition functions. Explore the limits of what can be computed.

overview.overviewText: A Turing Machine is a mathematical model of computation that defines an abstract machine which manipulates symbols on a strip of tape according to a table of rules. It provides a simple yet powerful framework for understanding what problems can be solved algorithmically.

exercises.exerciseWorksheetAlternatingSymbolsDesc: Given a binary word over {0, 1}, construct a Turing machine that checks whether 0 and 1 always alternate, halting as soon as two equal symbols follow each other or the end of the input is reached.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetSwapFirstTwoSymbolsDesc: Construct a Turing machine that swaps the first two input symbols, leaves all remaining symbols unchanged, and finishes on the third symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetSetFirstAndLastToOne: Set First and Last Symbol to 1
exercises.exerciseWorksheetSetFirstAndLastToOneDes: Construct a Turing machine that overwrites the first and last input symbols with 1, leaves all other symbols unchanged, and finishes on the last input symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetAlternatingOverwriteDes: Construct a Turing machine that overwrites the input from left to right with alternating 0 and 1 symbols and finishes on the last input symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetOverwriteLastTwoWithZer: Set the Last Two Symbols to 0
Construct a Turing machine that overwrites the last two input symbols with 0 and finishes on the last input symbol.
exercises.exerciseWorksheetAsciiParityBitDesc: Given an input of exactly seven bits, construct a Turing machine that counts the number of ones, writes the even-parity bit to the blank cell left of the input, and finishes on the first blank cell after the input.
exercises.exerciseEraseTapeDesc: Build a machine that replaces the whole input word with blanks and halts once the tape is cleared.
exercises.exerciseInvertBinaryWordDesc: Build a machine that flips every 0 to 1 and every 1 to 0, then halts on the first blank cell.
exercises.exerciseUnaryIncrementDesc: Build a machine that appends one additional 1 to the end of a unary word and then halts.
exercises.exerciseDuplicateZerosDesc: Construct a Turing machine that doubles the number of 0s on the tape when they are enclosed by two 1s. Examples: 101 -> 1001, 1001 -> 100001.
exercises.exerciseAddBinaryDesc: Construct a Turing machine that is able to add two numbers in binary representation. To simplify the task, you may make assumptions. For example, you may define that the first addend (the left one) is greater than the second addend, that the read head always starts on the first input symbol, or that a specific symbol must appear between the numbers.
exercises.exerciseCheckRegexDesc: Given the regular expression R1 = (1(01)* | 0(10)*) construct a Turing machine that checks whether an arbitrary binary word can be described by R1. After execution, the tape must contain either a 't' for true or an 'f' for false. Example: The input 11001 cannot be represented by R1, so the tape contains an 'f' and everything else has been removed.
exercises.exerciseBinaryIncrementDesc: Build a machine that adds 1 to a binary number on the tape and halts with the incremented result.

examples.example1Desc: A complete machine that inverts every bit in a binary word while scanning from left to right.
examples.example2Desc: A compact machine that scans to the end of a unary word and writes one extra 1.
examples.example3Desc: A carry-based machine that increments a binary word by one.
examples.example4Desc: A complete binary-adder machine for inputs such as 101+11. Follow the tape states and transitions to see how the second addend is consumed and the result is built.

endsWith01.title: Strings ending with "01"
endsWith01.goal: Build a DFA that accepts binary strings ending with "01".
endsWith01.description: Design a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts exactly those strings whose last two symbols are "0" followed by "1" (e.g. "01", "101", "1001"). Strings ending in any other pattern must be rejected.
endsWith01.hint1: Track how much of the pattern "01" you have matched so far. Three states are enough: nothing, just saw a 0, just saw "01".
endsWith01.hint2: From the accept state, reading a 0 should fall back to "just saw a 0" (you might still be on track), and reading a 1 should reset to "nothing".

endsWith00.title: Strings ending with "00"
endsWith00.goal: Build a DFA that accepts binary strings ending with two zeros.
endsWith00.description: Design a DFA over {0, 1} that accepts exactly those strings whose last two symbols are both 0 (e.g. "00", "100", "1100"). Single zeros or strings ending in 1 must be rejected.
endsWith00.hint1: You need to remember how many trailing zeros you have just seen. Three states (0, 1, or 2 trailing zeros) are enough.
endsWith00.hint2: From the "two trailing zeros" state, reading another 0 should stay there, but reading a 1 should jump back to "zero trailing zeros".

evenOnes.title: Even number of 1s
evenOnes.goal: Accept binary strings containing an even number of 1s (including zero 1s).
evenOnes.description: Design a DFA that tracks the parity of 1s seen so far. The empty string should be accepted (zero is even).
evenOnes.hint1: You only need two states — one for "even" and one for "odd".
evenOnes.hint2: Reading 0 never changes the parity, but reading 1 always flips it.

noConsecOnes.title: No two consecutive 1s
noConsecOnes.goal: Accept binary strings that never contain "11" as a substring.
noConsecOnes.description: Design a DFA that rejects any string in which two 1s appear next to each other. Strings like "0", "01", "010" are accepted; "11", "0110" are rejected.
noConsecOnes.hint1: Track whether the last symbol you read was a 1. Reading another 1 immediately after must lead to a dead state.
noConsecOnes.hint2: A dead (trap) state has self-loops on every symbol and is not accepting.

divBy3.title: Binary numbers divisible by 3
divBy3.goal: Accept binary strings whose decimal value is divisible by 3.
divBy3.description: Build a DFA that tracks the running remainder of the binary value modulo 3. Accept the states representing remainder 0.
divBy3.hint1: You only need three states — one for each possible remainder (0, 1, 2).
divBy3.hint2: When you are in state with remainder r and read bit b, the new remainder is (2·r + b) mod 3.
divBy3.hint3: The start state and the single accept state are both the same: remainder 0.

exerciseWorkspace.confirmBody: Your current automaton will be replaced with the reference solution. You can still reset the exercise from the Exercises tab.

endsWith01.title: Binary strings ending in 01
endsWith01.description: A DFA that accepts all binary strings that end with the substring "01". This is one of the most common introductory DFA examples.
endsWith01.step1: We want to accept exactly those binary strings that end with "01". The automaton must remember whether the last two symbols it read were "0" followed by "1".
endsWith01.step2: We need three states: s0 (start — haven't seen the start of "01" yet), s1 (just read a "0" — could be the first part of "01"), and s2 (just read "01" — accept state).
endsWith01.step3: From s0: reading "0" moves to s1 (potential start of "01"), reading "1" stays in s0. From s1: reading "1" moves to s2 (we found "01"!), reading "0" stays in s1 (new potential start). From s2: reading "0" moves to s1, reading "1" goes back to s0.
endsWith01.step4: The automaton always tracks how much of the pattern "01" has been matched so far. No matter how long the string is, it only needs 3 states because it only cares about the last two characters. This is the power of finite automata — they can recognize patterns with constant memory.

evenOnes.title: Even number of 1s
evenOnes.description: A DFA that accepts binary strings containing an even number of 1s (including zero 1s). A classic example of parity checking.
evenOnes.step1: We want to accept strings where the count of '1' symbols is even (0, 2, 4, ...). The automaton just needs to track the parity (even or odd) of 1s seen so far — it doesn't need to count them exactly.
evenOnes.step2: Only two states are needed: 'even' (we have seen an even number of 1s) and 'odd' (we have seen an odd number of 1s). The start state is 'even' because zero 1s is even. The accept state is also 'even'.
evenOnes.step3: Reading a '0' never changes the parity, so both states loop back to themselves on '0'. Reading a '1' flips the parity: even→odd and odd→even. That's the entire automaton!

containsAba.title: Contains substring "aba"
containsAba.description: An NFA that accepts any string over {a, b} that contains "aba" as a substring anywhere within it. Demonstrates nondeterminism.
containsAba.step1: We want to accept any string that contains "aba" somewhere inside it. Before and after the pattern, any combination of 'a' and 'b' is allowed.
containsAba.step2: An NFA is natural here because we don't know when "aba" starts. The NFA can "guess" nondeterministically — in state s0, when it reads 'a', it both stays in s0 (in case this isn't the start of the pattern) AND moves to s1 (in case it is). If any path leads to acceptance, the string is accepted.
containsAba.step3: Four states: s0 (haven't started matching), s1 (matched "a"), s2 (matched "ab"), s3 (matched "aba" — accept state, stays here forever on any input).
containsAba.step4: In a DFA, we'd need to carefully track partial matches and overlaps. With the NFA, we simply "try all possibilities" at once. The simulator tracks all active states in parallel, showing how the NFA explores multiple paths simultaneously.

epsilonNfa.title: NFA with ε-transitions
epsilonNfa.description: An NFA that uses epsilon (ε) transitions — transitions that happen without reading any input symbol. Demonstrates spontaneous state changes.
epsilonNfa.step1: An ε-transition allows the automaton to move from one state to another without consuming an input symbol. This means the automaton can be in multiple states simultaneously even before reading any input.
epsilonNfa.step2: Before processing starts, we compute the ε-closure of the start state — all states reachable by following ε-transitions from q0. Here, q0 has an ε-transition to q1, so the initial active states are {q0, q1}.
epsilonNfa.step3: q0 reads 'a's and can spontaneously jump to q1 via ε. q1 reads one 'b' and moves to q2. q2 spontaneously jumps to q3 via ε. q3 is the accept state and accepts any remaining input.
epsilonNfa.step4: ε-transitions make it easier to combine automata (e.g., for union or concatenation of languages). They don't add computational power — every NFA with ε-transitions can be converted to one without — but they make automaton construction more modular and intuitive.

divisibleBy3.title: Binary numbers divisible by 3
divisibleBy3.description: A DFA that accepts binary numbers whose decimal value is divisible by 3. An elegant example showing how automata can perform arithmetic.
divisibleBy3.step1: We want to accept binary strings that represent numbers divisible by 3 (remainder 0 when divided by 3). For example: "0" (0), "11" (3), "110" (6), "1001" (9) should all be accepted.
divisibleBy3.step2: When reading a binary number left-to-right, each new bit doubles the current value and adds the new bit. So if the current value is V and we read bit b, the new value is 2V + b. We only care about V mod 3, which has just 3 possible values: 0, 1, or 2.
divisibleBy3.step3: Three states represent the three possible remainders: s0 (remainder 0 — accept state), s1 (remainder 1), s2 (remainder 2). The start state is s0 because we start with value 0, which has remainder 0.
divisibleBy3.step4: For each state (remainder r) and input bit b: new remainder = (2r + b) mod 3. For example: from s1 reading '0': (2×1+0) mod 3 = 2 → go to s2. From s1 reading '1': (2×1+1) mod 3 = 0 → go to s0. This mathematical derivation gives us a complete, correct transition table.

lecture.title: Lecture Example
lecture.description: A DFA from the lecture exercise that accepts one or more '0's followed by exactly one '1' (Regex: 0+1).
lecture.step1: The automaton requires at least one '0', followed by exactly one '1', and then nothing else. It rejects empty strings, strings starting with '1', or strings with more than one '1'.
lecture.step2: s0 is the start state. Reading '0' moves to s1 (we have our 0s). From s1, reading '1' moves to s2 (the accept state). Any other input leads to s3, which is a "sink" or "trap" state because the string is invalid.

grammar.title: Grammar → Automat
grammar.description: The right-linear grammar G = {S → 0S | 0A, A → 1A | 1} is converted into an NFA and then into a minimal DFA via subset construction. Both recognize the language L = {0ⁿ 1ᵐ | n,m ≥ 1}.
grammar.step1: Construct a finite automaton for the regular grammar: G = {S → 0S | 0A, A → 1A | 1} over Σ = {0, 1}. This grammar generates '0's then '1's. Each non-terminal becomes a state, and each production becomes a transition.
grammar.step2: Map productions to transitions: (S → 0S) becomes δ(S,0)=S; (S → 0A) becomes δ(S,0)=A. This creates non-determinism at state S on input '0'. The rule (A → 1) implies a transition to a dedicated accept state (sF). Result: A 3-state NFA {S, A, sF}.
grammar.step3:
We group NFA states into sets to ensure one transition per input.
1. Start at q0 = {S}.
2. Move on '0': δ(q0, 0) = {S, A} → new state q1.
3. Move on '1': δ(q0, 1) = ∅ → sink state qD.
4. δ(q1, 0) = {S, A} → loops back to q1.
5. δ(q1, 1) = {A, sF} → new state q2.
6. δ(q2, 0) = ∅ → qD. δ(q2, 1) = {A, sF} → loops back to q2.
q2 is the accept state (contains sF). qD is a dead/trap state.
